rubrics.title: Queen Mary University of London undergraduate marking scheme and degree classification (College-wide)
rubrics.body:
MARK SCALE
Assessments are marked to integers; module marks and the Classification Mark are held to one decimal place. Queen Mary's generic undergraduate scheme (Assessment Handbook 2026-27 para 5.31):
A 70.0-100.0 Excellent (First Class)
B 60.0-69.9 Good (Second Class, Upper Division)
C 50.0-59.9 Satisfactory (Second Class, Lower Division)
D 40.0-49.9 Pass (threshold pass) (Third Class)
F 0.0-39.9 Fail
The module pass mark is normally 40.0. It is 50.0 for level 7 undergraduate modules and for the MBBS, BDS, BSc Oral Health and FdCert Clinical Foundation Studies; there is then no D grade and F runs from 0.0-49.9. (Before 2024-25 the scheme had an E grade, 40.0-44.9, and D was 45.0-49.9.)

ATTEMPTS, RESITS AND FAILED CREDIT
A student has a maximum of two attempts at a module (first attempt and one resit); a passed resit is capped at the pass mark. If both attempts fail, the higher ('best fail') mark stands. Core modules must be taken and passed. Standard bachelor's progression: take 120 credits a year (at least 90 at the year's level), pass at least 90 credits in year one with a weighted average year mark of 40.0 or higher, pass at least 195 credits across years one and two with a weighted average of 40.0 or higher (1:3 weighting), and fail (after resit) no more than 30 credits in any developmental year. Undergraduate rules do not provide compensation of failed modules; instead the award requires 360 credits taken, at least 315 passed (including at least 90 at level 6 or higher) and a Classification Mark of 40.0 or higher. Integrated master's students need a weighted average of 60.0 or higher (years weighted 1:3:6) to proceed to the final year; a Subject Examination Board may exceptionally allow 57.0 or higher.

HOW THE CLASS IS CALCULATED
The Classification Mark is an aggregate weighted by module credit. Standard bachelor's (BA, BSc, BEng, LLB, BSc (Econ)): year one 10%, year two 30%, final year 60% (1:3:6). Integrated master's (MEng, MSci): 1:3:6:6, i.e. 6.25%, 18.75%, 37.5%, 37.5%.

CLASS BANDS
70.0-100.0 First Class (Honours)
60.0-69.9 Second Class (Honours) (Upper Division)
50.0-59.9 Second Class (Honours) (Lower Division)
40.0-49.9 Third Class (Honours)
Borderline policy: a student with a Classification Mark within 1.5 of a class boundary (except the pass/fail border) is in the zone of consideration, and is raised to the higher class if at least half of their final-year credits carry marks at the level of the higher class (or above). There is no discretion at the pass/fail border.

HOW MARKING MUST BE DONE
Marking must be criterion-referenced (not norm-referenced) and must never seek to represent a student's potential. Schools and institutes apply marking criteria with reference to their discipline, level and assessment type; these must align with Queen Mary's generic scheme, and any divergence must be explained to students. The marking scheme must be communicated to students clearly and in advance. At least 50% of each module's assessment (by weighting) goes through blind or open double marking, mark checking, electronic marking or moderation; dissertations and projects must be double marked. Where two markers differ by 10% of the marks available or less they may split the difference; otherwise a third mark stands. Scaling solely to meet predefined norms is never acceptable.

USING THIS RUBRIC
Queen Mary's College-wide scheme gives only the one-word descriptors above (Excellent / Good / Satisfactory / Pass / Fail); fuller qualitative descriptors are set by each School. Use the School's criteria where available and map the result onto these bands.
rubrics.source_note: Queen Mary Academic Regulations 2026-27: paras 2.66, 2.80-2.88 (pass marks, attempts, resit cap, best fail), 2.113-2.115 (Classification Mark, borderline policy), 4.26-4.33 (bachelor's progression, award, 1:3:6 weighting, class bands), 4.39-4.44 (integrated master's). Queen Mary Assessment Handbook 2026-27, section 5 (paras 5.8, 5.25-5.33 generic scheme and criterion referencing; 5.37-5.55 quality assurance, moderation and marker disagreement): https://www.qmul.ac.uk/governance-and-legal-services/media/dgls-media/policy/2026-27-policies/Assessment-Handbook-2026-27.pdf. Cross-checked against the 2025-26 Regulations and Assessment Handbook, which contain the same provisions; the 2026-27 summary of changes lists no change to UG pass marks, weightings, boundaries or borderline rules.

rubrics.title: School of the Arts marking criteria (Queen Mary University of London)
rubrics.body:
Apply the section that matches the module's subject.

SECTION 1. ENGLISH AND DRAMA (English, Drama, Creative Writing)
HOW WORK IS JUDGED
The School follows Queen Mary's assessment and marking policies: marking is criterion-referenced, at least 50% of each module's assessment is internally moderated or double marked, and an external examiner reviews a sample. Markers in English and Drama consider three main areas: (1) Knowledge and Understanding; (2) Engagement and Analysis; (3) Expression and Presentation. The assignment mark takes all three into consideration, and the work must follow the brief. Scale: A 70+ Excellent, B 60-69.9 Good, C 50-59.9 Satisfactory, D 40-49.9 Adequate, F 0-39.9 Fail.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
90-100 (A) EXCEPTIONAL: as with 80-89, but in a manner that far exceeds what is expected of a student working at this module's level, in all three areas.

80-89 (A) OUTSTANDING: identifies relevant material comprehensively and independently; understands and applies relevant ideas, concepts, contexts and practices in nuanced ways. Deep engagement with appropriate materials that goes beyond what the assignment expected; analysis focused, convincing, wide-ranging and ambitious; the response is original and challenges or extends existing scholarship and/or creative practice. Presentation impeccable in all formal respects; style exceeds what is expected at this level; the work could be of interest to a professional (academic or creative) audience.

70-79 (A) EXCELLENT: identifies relevant material comprehensively; understands and applies relevant ideas, concepts, contexts and practices thoroughly. Deep engagement with appropriate materials; analysis focused and convincing; makes original contributions to existing scholarship and/or creative practice. Very well structured and organised, the argument or creative logic systematically developed; strong command of appropriate expression; follows the required style (e.g. the QMUL English and Drama Style Guide).

60-69 (B) GOOD: identifies, understands and applies relevant materials, ideas, concepts and practices accurately. Selects and analyses materials with care; aware of complexities in the relevant ideas or practices; often engages with relevant arguments and concepts. Well organised and convincingly structured; style appropriate and consistent, fully meeting expectations for the level; follows the required style, perhaps with a small number of minor errors.

50-59 (C) SATISFACTORY: identifies relevant material sometimes, though some could be better chosen; understands and applies relevant ideas sometimes. Some use of relevant materials; some coherent elements to the analysis; response adequate but some elements underdeveloped. Follows a structure but with some problems of organisation; style consistent but expression just meets expectations; citations and references present but often not in accordance with the Style Guide.

40-49 (D) ADEQUATE: identifies, understands and applies relevant material and ideas infrequently. Many materials chosen are not appropriate; analysis often incomplete or lacking coherence; relies extensively on the work of others or falls below the module level's expectations. Aims often difficult to understand; style often inappropriate or below expectations; often does not follow the required style.

0-39 (F) FAIL: identifies little or no relevant material; understands and applies relevant ideas minimally or not at all. Materials not appropriate; analysis incomplete and incoherent; engages with relevant material minimally or not at all. Presentation below the standard expected, with frequent errors (grammar, spelling, speech); little or no attempt to follow the required style.

SECTION 2. LANGUAGES, LINGUISTICS, FILM AND COMPARATIVE LITERATURE
HOW WORK IS JUDGED (NON-LANGUAGE MODULES)
Examiners bear in mind a number of criteria when determining a mark, including how fully the relevant issues are covered, understanding of the critical literature, how clearly and convincingly arguments are made and supported, and originality. Weakness in one area may be offset by strength in another. Narrative or descriptive essays, rather than analytical ones, will not normally be graded higher than C. Criteria: following the brief and handling key terms; knowledge and understanding; argument, analysis and use of critical literature; structure; language; referencing; presentation.

WHAT EACH GRADE LOOKS LIKE
A (70-100): follows the brief, confident with key terms (may productively challenge and question them); excellent knowledge/understanding of the topic, the wider subject area, theory and material beyond the module; a coherent line of argument backed up with excellent analysis, going beyond the critical literature and showing original thinking; an appropriate and elegant structure; excellent command of language (accurate grammar, scholarly register, fluency); impeccable referencing and bibliography; excellent presentation (e.g. 11-point font, 1.5 line spacing, numbered pages).
90-100 Exceptional: significantly exceeds the A threshold; sophisticated, original and authoritative analysis; immaculate presentation; at the top of the range, needs no further improvement.
80-89 Outstanding: clearly exceeds the threshold; unusually thorough understanding and original analysis; minor areas still to improve.
70-79 Excellent: meets or exceeds the threshold; thorough understanding and sophisticated analysis; elements could still be developed.

B (60-69): follows the brief, confident with key terms and concepts; good knowledge/understanding of the topic, wider subject area and theoretical approaches; coherent argument backed by good analysis, with good understanding and synthesis of the critical literature; appropriate structure, good organisation; good grammar, spelling and punctuation in a suitable scholarly register; good referencing and presentation.

C (50-59): follows the brief, satisfactory handling of key terms; satisfactory knowledge of topic and wider subject; an identifiable argument with satisfactory analysis, but some problems synthesising the critical literature; functional structure; reasonably accurate language in a suitable register; satisfactory referencing and presentation.

D (40-49): does not always stick to the task, problems handling key terms; adequate knowledge of the topic but weak knowledge of the wider subject; adequate but poorly integrated argument and analysis, problems synthesising literature; adequate but incoherent structure; inaccurate spelling, grammar and punctuation, no suitable scholarly register; inconsistent or incomplete referencing; only adequate presentation (e.g. not word-processed, unnumbered pages).

F (0-39): does not stick to the task, severe problems with key terms; little or no knowledge; no argument or analysis and no understanding of the critical literature; non-existent structure; very poor command of language (possibly unreadable); no references or bibliography, possibly plagiarised material; extremely poor presentation.

LANGUAGE MODULES
Written target-language work is assessed with CEFR-based tables (A1/A2, B1/B2, C1/C2) and a translation table, in bands 85-100, 70-84, 60-69, 50-59, 40-49 and 39 and below, covering grammar, vocabulary, spelling/punctuation, fluency and coherence (at C1/C2 content and command of language are weighted 50% each). E.g. B1/B2: 85-100 outstanding accuracy and exceptional vocabulary; 60-69 good grammar, minor errors, style may be clumsy but argument clear; 40-49 considerable grammar problems, may struggle to produce comprehensible text; 39 and below extremely poor, basic communication at risk.
